n: Hezekiah became king at twenty-five and reigned twenty-nine years (about 715–686 BC). His mother was Abijah, daughter of Zechariah.
He did right in God’s sight just as David had — high praise reserved for very few kings.

f.w: according to all that David his father had done

n: In the very first month of his reign, Hezekiah reopened and repaired the temple doors his father had shut. He made restoring worship his first priority.
He gathered the priests and Levites in the square on the east side of the temple.

f.g: An open square east of the temple.

n: He commanded the Levites to purify themselves and the temple and carry out the defilement — the idols and debris from Ahaz’s reign. Personal purity comes before cleansing God’s house.

f.g: Ritually unclean things — idols and their equipment.

n: Hezekiah openly confesses: our fathers sinned, forsook God, and turned their backs on His house. Honest confession begins renewal.
They had shut the doors, put out the lamps, and stopped incense and burnt offerings — silencing the house of God.

f.g: The lampstand was to burn continually before the Lord.

n: So God’s anger came on Judah, making it a horror and a thing people hissed at, as everyone could see.

f.g: A sound of contempt and shock.

n: Our fathers died in battle, and our families are in captivity because of this.
Hezekiah resolves to make a covenant with the Lord so His fierce anger may turn away. Renewal comes through covenant.
He addresses the Levites tenderly as “my sons”: don’t be negligent now — God chose you to stand before Him and serve.
Levites from all three main clans — Kohath, Merari, and Gershon — responded, two leaders from each.
Also from the clan of Elizaphan and from the singing family of Asaph.
And from the singer families of Heman and Jeduthun. Fourteen leaders in all stepped up.
They gathered their brothers, purified themselves, and began cleansing the temple as the king commanded, following the Lord’s word.

f.w: by the words of the LORD
f.g: According to the law God had given.

n: The priests cleaned the inner rooms and brought everything unclean out to the courtyard; the Levites carried it out to the Kidron Valley.
The work began on the first day of the first month; in eight days they reached the porch, and in eight more they finished — sixteen days in all.

f.w: the first day of the first month
f.g: The month of Nisan, when Passover would normally be held on the 14th.

n: They reported to Hezekiah that the whole temple, the altar, the bread table, and their utensils were cleansed.
They had also restored and purified the vessels Ahaz had discarded, and set them before the altar.
Early the next morning Hezekiah gathered the city’s leaders and went up to the temple.
They brought seven each of bulls, rams, lambs, and goats as a sin offering for the kingdom, the sanctuary, and Judah. Seven signals completeness.
Priests slaughtered the animals and sprinkled their blood on the altar.
The goats for the sin offering were brought before the king and assembly, who laid hands on them — symbolically transferring their sins to the offering.

f.w: they laid their hands upon them

n: The priests made atonement with the goats’ blood for “all Israel” — including the northern tribes. Hezekiah wanted to reunite God’s whole people. These sacrifices pointed to Christ’s atoning blood.

f.w: to make an atonement for all Israel

n: He stationed Levites with cymbals, lyres, and harps, as commanded by David and the prophets Gad and Nathan — for the music too came by revelation.

f.w: for so was the commandment of the LORD by his prophets

n: The Levites stood with David’s instruments and the priests with trumpets.
As the burnt offering began, so did the “song of the LORD,” with trumpets and instruments. Sacrifice and song went together.
The whole assembly worshipped while singers sang and trumpets sounded until the offering was finished.
Afterward the king and all present bowed and worshipped.
Hezekiah had the Levites sing praises with the words of David and Asaph — psalms we still have — and they sang joyfully and bowed in worship.

f.g: Asaph is credited with Psalms 50 and 73–83.

n: Hezekiah invited the people, now consecrated, to bring sacrifices and thank offerings. Many, with willing hearts, brought burnt offerings too.
The people brought 70 bulls, 100 rams, and 200 lambs as burnt offerings.
Other consecrated offerings totaled 600 cattle and 3,000 sheep.
There weren’t enough purified priests to skin all the offerings, so Levites helped, because the Levites had been more diligent in purifying themselves than the priests.
With abundant offerings, fat of peace offerings, and drink offerings, temple worship was restored in proper order.
Hezekiah and the people rejoiced at how God had prepared them, for it all happened so quickly. Rapid renewal was itself God’s gift.
